overview.title: Help game characters navigate a level
overview.description: An NPC can search a maze, a tactical grid, or a voxel level for a legal route. The map and movement rules determine whether the character can move diagonally, cross terrain, or pass through a cell.
overview.project_note: MovingAI and Monash profiles include game-derived maps. They are map collections, not evaluations inside a game engine.

overview.title: Route across a road network
overview.description: A route can minimize distance or travel time across directed streets. Edge direction, turn rules, and cost units change what the shortest route means.
overview.project_note: DIMACS road graphs form a separate benchmark cohort with explicit distance and time weights.

overview.title: Coordinate movement through shared bottlenecks
overview.description: Carts, game units, or route abstractions may need to share narrow aisles and passages without blocking one another. Each route depends on where other agents are and when they arrive.
overview.project_note: EECBS and LaCAM* cover graph-based multi-agent coordination. They do not model pedestrian behavior or validate evacuation safety.

overview.title: Plan a maneuver a car can actually drive
overview.description: A car-like agent needs to account for heading, turning radius, and body clearance. A geometrically short line may be impossible for the vehicle to follow.
overview.project_note: Hybrid A* and State Lattice demonstrate curvature-bounded vehicle motions in a modeled space; they are not a validated driving stack.

overview.title: Move through a crowded workcell
overview.description: An arm's route is a sequence of joint configurations. Collision checking must account for the shape swept by the arm, not only the path of its endpoint.
overview.project_note: The site catalogs OMPL problem resources and configurations; no OMPL planner runs are included in the recorded campaigns.

overview.title: Find a low-cost route through connected systems
overview.description: The same graph-search questions apply to weighted links between routers, services, or infrastructure sites: which states are reachable, what does each link cost, and how should the route respond to change?
overview.project_note: Network routing is a model analogy here; no computer-network dataset is part of the current benchmark collection.

discrete.title: Game maps and NPC navigation
discrete.scenario: A character needs a legal route through a maze, tactical grid, or terrain map.
discrete.connection: Grid and graph search make the movement rules explicit. MovingAI and Monash profiles provide map examples, while the exact game behavior remains outside this project.

discrete.title: Road and transit routing
discrete.scenario: A traveler needs the least-distance or least-time route across a directed network.
discrete.connection: Dijkstra and A* reason over edge costs and direction. DIMACS road graphs are evaluated as a distinct cohort because distance and time are different objectives.

discrete.title: Service and communication networks
discrete.scenario: A request needs a low-cost route through connected services or links.
discrete.connection: The graph abstraction transfers directly, but real network congestion, reliability, and changing capacity need additional models and data.

continuous.title: Car-like vehicle maneuvers
continuous.scenario: A vehicle must turn through a tight space without exceeding its steering limits.
continuous.connection: Hybrid A* and State Lattice model poses and curvature-bounded local motions in SE(2); collision checks also account for a footprint.

continuous.title: Robot arms in workcells
continuous.scenario: A manipulator must move between joint configurations while avoiding surrounding equipment.
continuous.connection: Sampling-based planners search a configuration space, but the result depends on a correct robot model and collision-validity checks.

continuous.title: Geometric inspection routes
continuous.scenario: An inspection platform needs a collision-free route through a modeled free space.
continuous.connection: Sampling, roadmaps, and informed search provide reusable ideas. Platform dynamics, sensing, and operating constraints must be modeled separately.

temporal.title: Routes around time-dependent blockages
temporal.scenario: A passage is unavailable for part of the schedule, so an agent may need to wait before crossing.
temporal.connection: SIPP searches safe time intervals instead of treating every moment as a separate graph node.

temporal.title: Timed crossings and shared corridors
temporal.scenario: A vehicle or automated cart must pass a crossing only when the shared space is free.
temporal.connection: Time windows and traversal duration matter alongside distance. Coordinating many agents requires an additional multi-agent model.

temporal.title: Schedule-aware mobility
temporal.scenario: A route must respect opening times, temporary closures, or a required arrival window.
temporal.connection: Temporal planners can represent availability constraints when they are supplied as safe intervals; timetable quality and service policy remain external inputs.

multi_agent.title: Warehouse fleet coordination
multi_agent.scenario: Several carts share narrow aisles and must avoid occupying the same node or swapping across the same edge.
multi_agent.connection: EECBS and LaCAM* search for conflict-free paths on a shared graph under explicit movement and goal rules.

multi_agent.title: Groups of game units
multi_agent.scenario: Multiple units need routes through one level without blocking each other at doors or bridges.
multi_agent.connection: Joint-state and conflict-based methods expose interactions that independent single-agent routes miss.

multi_agent.title: Pedestrian flow abstractions
multi_agent.scenario: A graph model can explore how routes interact at shared passages or bottlenecks.
multi_agent.connection: This abstraction does not capture human behavior, density, accessibility, or emergency safety; those need validated domain models.
